new_statements.quote: Binnen die Indo-europese talen maakt het Nederlands weer deel uit van de Germaanse talen. Deze groep onderscheidt zich van de rest door een paar specifieke verschijnselen. De belangrijkste daarvan zijn de volgende. [...] 2. De verschuiving van het accent naar de eerste lettergreep - met als uitzondering de geprefigeerde werkwoorden. Dit had grote gevolgen voor de uitgangen van de woorden, daar de neiging bestond die steeds meer te laten afzwakken. Deze verschuiving van het accent is jonger dan de eerste klankverschuiving (zie onder 1. Wet van Verner). [p. 47:] Door de verplaatsing van het accent naar de beginlettergreep ontstond binnen alle Germaanse talen een tendens om de naamval ... niet meer met uitgangen maar met behulp van voorzetsels en lidwoorden aan te duiden.
new_statements.translation: Within the Indo-European languages Dutch in turn belongs to the Germanic languages. This group is distinguished from the rest by a few specific phenomena. The most important are the following. [...] 2. The shift of the accent to the first syllable - with the prefixed verbs as the exception. This had great consequences for the endings of words, since there was a tendency to let them weaken more and more. This accent shift is younger than the first sound shift (see under 1, Verner's Law). [p. 47:] Through the displacement of the accent to the initial syllable there arose in all Germanic languages a tendency to mark case ... no longer with endings but with prepositions and articles.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Old Dutch continues the Common Germanic fixed accent: main (dynamic) stress on the first syllable of the word, which is normally the root/stem syllable; prefixed verbs (be-, gi-/ge-, far-/fer- etc.) are the exception, carrying stress on the verbal root rather than the prefix, while nominal compounds/prefixed nouns stress the first element (cf. Schönfeld §88 verzórgen : vóorzorg, Mnl. belúiken : bíloke). Unstressed (non-initial) syllables undergo progressive vowel reduction toward schwa during the Old Dutch period.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated for Old Dutch by Quak 1997. Schönfeld/Van Loey §89 speaks of 'bijtonige' syllables with full vowels (heavy suffixes such as -ig, -lijk, -baar, -zaam; second members of compounds) that carried a secondary accent and later attracted main stress, dating at least one such shift (aanhóudend type) to the pre-Middle-Dutch period; Heyne p. 5 describes only a 'leichteres Hingleiten im Ton' over non-stem syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Prefixed verbs stress the root, not the prefix (Quak p. 38; Schönfeld §88; Van Bree p. 77); proclitic particles ne, te, be- are weakly stressed (Borgeld §6 Aant. 2). Later Dutch stress shifts (suffixal -ig/-lijk/-baar/-zaam, on- before adjectives, French loans, 'eenheidsaccent' in names) are described by Schönfeld §89 and Van Bree p. 77 as post-Germanic developments, mostly Middle/Modern Dutch.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent of inherited Germanic vocabulary, stated diachronically (Germanic accent shift inherited by Old Dutch) rather than as a synchronic description of the attested Old Dutch corpus (Wachtendonck Psalms, Leiden Willeram); the corpus grammars (Borgeld 1899, Quak 1997 §2.2) presuppose it by sorting vowels into stem/stressed vs unstressed syllables. Accent type characterised as predominantly dynamic/expiratory (Schönfeld §87).
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Old Dutch / Old Low Franconian (Oudnederlands, Altniederfränkisch), c. 900-1200, chiefly on the basis of the Wachtendonck Psalms (Old East Low Franconian, 10th c.) and the Leiden Willeram (c. 1100); this is the variety Glottolog codes as oldd1237 'Old Dutch-Old Frankish' (ISO odt). Heyne 1873 treats Old Low Franconian together with Old Saxon (olds1250) but the quoted sentence names altniederfränkisch explicitly. Schönfeld/Van Loey 1970 and Van Bree 1987 state the rule for Common Germanic > Dutch as a whole rather than for the Old Dutch stage specifically.

sources.locator: ch. 2.1, p. 38 (list of Germanic features inherited by Old Dutch, item 2); cf. p. 47 §2.2.2.1 and §2.2.1.3 'Klinkers' (beklemtoonde vs onbeklemtoonde lettergrepen). Corroborated by Heyne 1873 p. 5 and Schönfeld/Van Loey 1970 §§88-89 pp. 108-109.
sources.note: p. 38, listing the Germanic innovations that define the group Old Dutch belongs to: 'De verschuiving van het accent naar de eerste lettergreep - met als uitzondering de geprefigeerde werkwoorden', with weakening of endings as consequence; ch. 2.2.1.3 then organises the Old Dutch vowel system by 'beklemtoonde' vs 'onbeklemtoonde lettergrepen' and p. 47 repeats 'de verplaatsing van het accent naar de beginlettergreep'. No separate suprasegmental section.

sources.citation: Van Bree, C. 1987. Historische grammatica van het Nederlands. Dordrecht: Foris. Ch. 11 'Het Accent', p. 77; ch. 12 'De klanken in zwak geaccentueerde syllaben', p. 78ff.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 77: 'In het Ggm. ligt het (hoofd)accent in alle gevallen op de eerste syllabe van het woord', except prefixed verbs which stress the stem (Got. ándawaúrdi vs andwáurdjan; Dutch vóorzorg vs verzórgen, Mnl. bíloke vs belúiken); this Germanic state continues into Dutch, with later exceptions from rhythm and French loans. Framed for Germanic > Dutch generally, not Old Dutch specifically.

sources.citation: Schönfeld, M; bewerkt door A. Van Loey. 1970. Schönfeld's Historische grammatica van het Nederlands, 8e druk. Zutphen: Thieme. Derde hoofdstuk 'Het accent en de klanken van de syllaben zonder hoofdtoon', §§87-89, pp. 107-110.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: §88: in Common Germanic 'werd de klemtoon vooraan overheersend.. Daar nu in de regel de stamsyllabe de eerste was, kreeg deze gewoonlijk de hoofdtoon'; compound verbs stress the second member (verzórgen : vóorzorg); §89: 'In het ndl. is, in principe, het beginaccent van het ogm. bewaard gebleven', later shifts (-ig, -lijk, on-, loans) being post-Old-Dutch. Dynamic (expiratory) accent predominates in the Germanic/Dutch word accent (§87).

sources.citation: Borgeld, A. 1899. De Oudoostnederfrankische psalmen: klank- en vormleer. Proefschrift Groningen. Groningen: Wolters.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Klankleer is organised as I 'De vocalen der stamlettergrepen' vs II 'De vocalen der niet-behoofdtoonde lettergrepen' (§22ff), i.e. presupposes main stress on the stem syllable; §6 Aant. 2 attributes reduced ne/te/be- to 'zwakken klemtoon'. No explicit rule of accent placement stated.

sources.citation: Heyne, Moriz. 1873. Kleine altsächsische und altniederfränkische Grammatik. Paderborn: Schöningh. Erster Abschnitt (Lautlehre), p. 5.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 5: weakening of derivational and inflectional vowels is 'eine Folge des in den germanischen Sprachen auf der Stammsilbe festgehefteten Accents und des dadurch hervorgerufenen leichteren Hingleitens im Ton über andere Silben eines Wortes', and this weakening has reached a much higher degree 'im altsächsischen und noch mehr im altniederfränkischen'. No dedicated accent chapter.
